site.name: Ascott Allotments

myPlot.name: Starter Bed 11
myPlot.where: Starter Bed Community area, south-west corner by Station Gate (end of Long Lane)
myPlot.water: Water point right next to the starter beds
myPlot.woodChip: Free wood chip is delivered at the Ranelagh Rd and Queen Anne's Gardens gates, on the other side of the site

site.soil: Heavy yellow Ealing clay that waterlogs in winter. Compost goes on top and is never dug in.

membership.perks: Members get discounted seed potatoes, onion sets, shallots, garlic and more.

plot.note: About 3 × 3 m, north at the top. The beds and path take 2.85 m north to south; the strawberry row uses the last 15 cm along the slab path, so measure it on site. Which end is west is a guess: swap crops in the tracker if it's the other way round.

areas.side: South edge, along the slab path

Cloves 15 cm apart, rows 25 cm. Push into the compost, no hole in the cardboard. Arriving about 3–6 Nov.

15–20 cm apart. Calendula pots at this end (sow March–April) bring hoverflies against blackfly.

pots.where: Pots; on the plot in summer

weedGroups.name: Easy annuals
weedGroups.blurb: They die in winter. Pull them before they seed and they won't come back.

weedGroups.name: Check first: bindweed
weedGroups.blurb: Both come out, but two plants share the name. One is gone in a week, the other takes a season of pulling. Pull a stem gently and look at the root.

weedGroups.name: Possible problem: grass
weedGroups.blurb: A clump of grass is easy. Couch grass spreads by underground runners and regrows from every piece.

weeds.name: Fat hen
weeds.spot: Grey-green diamond leaves with a white mealy dust; grows tall and upright, seeds in dense spikes.
weeds.remove: Pull small ones. Cut big ones at ground level and leave the root in the soil to rot.
weeds.dispose: Compost if not in seed. Bag any plant with seed heads.

weeds.name: Redshank / knotgrass
weeds.spot: Redshank: red stems swollen at the joints, a dark blotch in the middle of each leaf, pink flower spikes. Knotgrass: low wiry mat with tiny leaves.
weeds.remove: Pull, or cut at the base. Knotgrass: cut the mat off at ground level; its root rots under cardboard.
weeds.dispose: Compost if not in seed. Bag seed heads.

weeds.name: Black medick / trefoil
weeds.spot: Low sprawl of clover-like leaves in threes, tiny yellow pom-pom flowers, black seed pods.
weeds.remove: Cut at ground level or just cover it. Its roots add nitrogen as they rot, so no need to get them out.

weeds.name: Chickweed
weeds.spot: Soft bright-green mats, small oval leaves in pairs, tiny white star flowers. Grows all winter.
weeds.remove: Rake it up by hand, or just cover it: cardboard smothers it.

weeds.name: Black bindweed
weeds.spot: Heart-shaped leaves, twining stems, tiny greenish flowers in clusters. Root: one thin, short root. No white runners.
weeds.remove: Pull and unwind it from whatever it climbs. The root is tiny, so nothing to dig.

weeds.name: Field bindweed
weeds.spot: Arrow-shaped leaves, white or pink trumpet flowers. Root: white, brittle, snaps easily and runs sideways deep in the soil.
weeds.remove: Don't dig: every broken root regrows, so digging spreads it. Expect shoots where roots were broken while clearing. Cover with cardboard and compost, then pull every shoot that appears, weekly. It weakens over a season or two once it can't feed.
weeds.dispose: Never compost pulled roots or shoots fresh. Drown them in a lidded bucket of water for 4+ weeks, then the sludge can go on the heap.

weeds.name: Grass tussocks
weeds.spot: A tight clump with a ball of fibrous roots. Pull it and nothing trails behind.
weeds.remove: Cut it down to the ground with shears, or slice the top off flat with the spade. Cardboard over the stump finishes it.
weeds.dispose: Stack upside down to rot down, or compost broken up. Bag seed heads.

weeds.name: Couch grass
weeds.spot: Grass that runs in lines, not clumps. Dig: wiry white runners with sharp pointed tips, new shoots at the joints.
weeds.remove: Don't dig or rotavate: it chops the runners into new plants. Cut it short, use a double layer of cardboard well overlapped, and pull any blades that find a gap.
weeds.dispose: Drown pulled runners in the lidded bucket, or bag them. Never compost them fresh.

weeds.name: Strawberries
weeds.spot: Toothed leaves in threes, runners rooting along the ground.
weeds.remove: Keep. Weed around them, cut off old brown leaves; pot up strong runners for new plants.

weeds.name: Lamb's ear
weeds.spot: Soft, furry silver leaves. Bees love the flower spikes.
weeds.remove: Keep, or move it to an edge. It spreads slowly; split it in spring if it gets big.

weeds.name: Sunflowers
weeds.spot: One big head per stem, a single thick root, no tubers.
weeds.remove: Let the heads dry for the birds or save seed, then pull the stems.

weeds.name: …or Jerusalem artichokes
weeds.spot: Looks like a sunflower with many smaller flowers. Scrape the soil at the base with your fingers: knobbly tubers mean artichokes.
weeds.remove: If tubers: lift them and eat them through winter (this is harvesting, not digging the bed). Any tuber left regrows, so decide whether they stay and where.
weeds.dispose: Eat the tubers. Stems to compost.

steps.title: Clear the seed heads
steps.body: Cut them off with shears or the sickle and bag them so they don't drop on the plot.

steps.title: Cut the rest at ground level
steps.body: No digging. Leave the roots in: they rot under the cardboard. The bindweed roots you've already broken will send up shoots; that's expected.

steps.title: Double layer of cardboard
steps.body: On both beds and the path. Stagger the joins, overlap 15 cm, and wet it well.

steps.title: 15 cm of compost on both beds
steps.body: About 1.1 m³, or 2 bulk bags. On heavy clay that waterlogs, the compost stays on top and is never dug in.

steps.title: Wood chip on the path
steps.body: Over the cardboard. It's free at the Ranelagh Rd and Queen Anne's Gardens gates.

steps.title: Plant
steps.body: Garlic, onions, beans and peas go straight into the compost with no hole in the cardboard. Cut an X only for strawberries and transplants like the chard plugs.

steps.title: Pull bindweed shoots weekly
steps.body: Any shoot that pokes through the cardboard or round the edges. Each one pulled starves the root.

notes: Covered ground doesn't count as cultivated.
Carpet is banned as a cover.
Water is off from the end of October to April.

groups.name: Ordered from Suttons
groups.sub: Arriving about 23–27 Oct; the garlic about 3–6 Nov. Tick each one when it arrives.

groups.name: Still to buy
groups.sub: Check the trading hut first: members pay less.

items.name: Insect mesh
items.why: Over the garlic and onions against allium leaf miner

items.name: Hoops
items.why: To hold up the mesh and the fleece

items.name: Cardboard
items.why: Double layer on both beds plus the path. Plain brown, tape and staples removed

items.name: Wood chip
items.why: For the path. Delivered free at the Ranelagh Rd and Queen Anne's Gardens gates

items.name: Stainless digging fork
items.why: For spreading compost and lifting crops, not for digging the beds

items.name: Shears or a kama sickle
items.why: Cutting weeds down to the ground

catalog.note: Months for London. In a cold spring wait a couple of weeks; the seed packet has the final say.

crops.name: Garlic
crops.about: A softneck garlic that stores until spring. It needs a cold winter to split into cloves, so autumn planting gives the biggest bulbs.
crops.grow: Push each clove, pointy end up, into the compost until the tip is 2–3 cm below the surface. No hole in the cardboard needed: the roots go through it.
crops.tip: Garlic hates competition, so keep it weeded. Lift it when the lower third of the leaves has gone yellow.

varieties.name: Solent Wight
varieties.why: The one you're growing: a softneck that stores well and rarely bolts.

varieties.name: Cristo
varieties.why: Softneck with a strong flavour and light aroma.

varieties.name: Germidour
varieties.why: Reliable softneck with large bulbs; can go in in autumn or spring.

varieties.name: Mersley Wight
varieties.why: The newest garlic AGM (2023), also fine planted in spring.

varieties.name: Carcassonne Wight
varieties.why: Pink-cloved hardneck, ready about a month before Solent Wight. Keeps only 4–6 months.

varieties.name: Arno
varieties.why: Softneck the RHS recommends because it keeps well.

crops.name: Autumn onion sets
crops.about: A Japanese overwintering onion. Planted in autumn, it's ready in June, weeks before onions planted in spring.
crops.grow: Push the sets into the compost with just the tips showing. Birds pull them out in the first fortnight; the mesh stops that.
crops.tip: Keep the mesh on: allium leaf miner lays eggs in October–November and again in March–April.

varieties.name: Senshyu
varieties.why: The one you're growing: a June gap-filler. Eat it within about a month.

varieties.name: Radar
varieties.why: Resists bolting well. A July crop that keeps until about September.

varieties.name: Shakespeare
varieties.why: British-bred brown onion; strong bolt resistance and stores well once cured.

varieties.name: Electric
varieties.why: Glossy red onion with red-streaked flesh; ready in June.

crops.name: Broad beans
crops.about: The hardiest broad bean and the one to sow in autumn. It flowers early, before most of the blackfly arrive.
crops.grow: Sow 5 cm deep straight into the compost. Push in a few canes and string as they grow; autumn beans get blown about in March winds.
crops.spacing: 15–20 cm apart in a double row
crops.tip: Pinch out the tips once the first pods set. It puts off blackfly, and the tips are good to eat.

varieties.name: Aquadulce Claudia
varieties.why: The one you're growing: the classic hardy autumn bean.

varieties.name: Aguadulce
varieties.why: Same top hardiness rating as Claudia; sow it in autumn or spring.

varieties.name: De Monica
varieties.why: Charles Dowding's pick for November sowing. A smaller plant, about 1.2 m.

varieties.name: Witkiem Manita
varieties.why: Fast-growing and early; best as a spring backup.

varieties.name: The Sutton
varieties.why: Dwarf bean, ideal for containers and windy sites.

varieties.name: Wizard
varieties.why: Small-seeded field bean. Dowding: "great over winter… tasty crop in May".

crops.name: Peas
crops.about: A very hardy, short pea for autumn sowing that grows to about 60 cm. Sweet peas to eat in May, well before spring-sown ones.
crops.grow: Sow 4–5 cm deep in a band 15 cm wide, straight into the compost. Push in twiggy sticks when you sow so the tendrils find them.
crops.tip: Mice dig up pea seed in winter. If the row comes up gappy, sow again in February.

varieties.name: Douce Provence
varieties.why: The one you're growing: a sweet, short pea for autumn sowing.

varieties.name: Meteor
varieties.why: Probably the hardiest pea of all. Dwarf (~45 cm) but less sweet.

varieties.name: Feltham First
varieties.why: Round-seeded first early, ~45 cm, needs little support.

varieties.name: Hurst Green Shaft
varieties.why: Tasty podding pea, about 1 m. Sow it in spring, not autumn.

varieties.name: Kelvedon Wonder
varieties.why: Reliable dwarf AGM pea for spring sowing.

crops.name: Lamb's lettuce
crops.about: Small rosettes of mild, soft leaves that sit through frost. The classic winter salad.
crops.grow: Sow thinly on the compost and cover with 1 cm of sieved compost. Under fleece it keeps growing slowly all winter.
crops.tip: Pick whole rosettes or a few leaves from each. Sow again in late summer for next winter.

varieties.name: Valentin
varieties.why: The best lamb's lettuce Charles Dowding has grown.

varieties.name: Vit
varieties.why: Vigorous, overwinters well, said to resist mildew. Bolts fast in summer.

varieties.name: Verte de Cambrai
varieties.why: Classic compact French type with very tender leaves.

varieties.name: Trophy
varieties.why: Dowding says it "looks promising".

crops.name: Land cress
crops.about: Peppery like watercress, but it grows in ordinary soil and shrugs off winter.
crops.grow: Sow thinly on the compost surface and cover lightly. It likes the damp, so clay suits it.
crops.tip: Keep it watered in summer or it runs to seed. Pick the outer leaves.

varieties.name: Land cress (the species)
varieties.why: No named varieties are sold in the UK. Dowding: an "excellent hardy plant" that crops all winter.

crops.name: Mizuna
crops.about: A Japanese mustard with feathery leaves. Cut it and it grows back several times.
crops.grow: Sow thinly in short rows on the compost. Cut leaves at 10 cm, leaving 3 cm stumps to regrow.
crops.spacing: Rows 15 cm apart, thinned to 5 cm
crops.tip: Flea beetles pepper it with holes in summer. Under fleece in winter it stays clean.

varieties.name: Kyoto
varieties.why: RHS: "well-flavoured and very hardy", sow all year. Leafier and slower to bolt.

varieties.name: Red Knight F1
varieties.why: Red-topped leaves that colour best in winter; slower to bolt.

varieties.name: Plain mizuna
varieties.why: Cheap and vigorous; Dowding buys his oriental leaves from CN Seeds.

crops.name: Chard
crops.about: Colourful stems and leaves like spinach. Plugs planted in autumn crop through a mild winter and come back strongly in spring.
crops.grow: Cut an X in the cardboard, fold the flaps under and plant the plug into the compost. Water it in.
crops.tip: Pick the outer leaves and leave the middle to keep growing. It flowers and finishes in late spring.

varieties.name: Perpetual Spinach
varieties.why: Leaf beet. Long-cropping, resists bolting, and the hardiest of the chards.

varieties.name: Fordhook Giant
varieties.why: White stems, the hardiest kind. A July sowing crops until March.

varieties.name: Bright Lights
varieties.why: Mixed red, yellow and orange stems; good as baby leaves too.

varieties.name: Rhubarb Chard
varieties.why: Bright red stalks and puckered leaves.

varieties.name: Charlotte
varieties.why: Dark green leaves with red veins and stalks.

crops.name: Winter lettuce
crops.about: Lettuces bred to sit through winter and heart up or regrow early in spring.
crops.grow: Plant module plugs into the fleeced bed. Pick outer leaves rather than cutting whole heads.
crops.tip: Slugs are the main winter threat on wet clay; Grenoble Red is the most slug-resistant.

varieties.name: Grenoble Red
varieties.why: Dowding's winter favourite "for resistance to frost, slugs and mildew".

varieties.name: Winter Density
varieties.why: Dark green semi-cos; the only winter lettuce with an AGM.

varieties.name: Arctic King
varieties.why: Butterhead "bred for autumn sowing with exceptional cold resistance" (RHS).

varieties.name: Valdor
varieties.why: Very hardy and slow to bolt.

crops.name: Rocket
crops.about: Peppery leaves. Salad rocket sown in September overwinters; wild rocket is a tougher perennial.
crops.grow: Sow under the fleece now, or plant plugs. Cut leaves at 8–10 cm.
crops.tip: Flea beetles hole it in summer; under fleece in winter it stays clean.

varieties.name: Salad rocket (Bingenheim)
varieties.why: Dowding: "especially the selection from Bingenheim". Overwinters from a September sowing.

varieties.name: Apollo
varieties.why: Larger, less lobed leaves (Dowding).

varieties.name: Wild rocket 'Dragon's Tongue'
varieties.why: Red-veined perennial, resilient and slow to bolt.

crops.name: Claytonia
crops.about: Winter purslane, or miner's lettuce: mild, succulent leaves that Dowding picks outdoors in December.
crops.grow: Sow under the fleece or plant plugs. Cut at 5 cm and it regrows.
crops.tip: It seeds itself in spring, so you rarely need to sow it twice.

varieties.name: Claytonia (the species)
varieties.why: No named varieties are sold. "Super-hardy", and regrows from 5 cm stumps.

crops.name: Oriental mustards
crops.about: Hot, colourful leaves that keep growing through mild winters and give salads a kick.
crops.grow: Plant plugs into the fleeced bed; pick leaves small for salad, bigger for cooking.
crops.tip: They taste hotter as the weather gets colder.

varieties.name: Green in Snow
varieties.why: "Top pungency" (Dowding); bred for cold tolerance.

varieties.name: Red Frills
varieties.why: "Pretty and of great flavour" (Dowding). Feathery red leaves.

varieties.name: Red Giant
varieties.why: Big purple leaves, best cooked.

varieties.name: Red Dragon
varieties.why: Dowding's salad mustard.

crops.name: Winter spinach
crops.about: Sown in late summer, it gives leaves in autumn and a big flush in early spring.
crops.grow: Plant module plugs now; pick the outer leaves.
crops.tip: Spinach bolts in summer but rarely in winter, which makes it a better winter crop.

varieties.name: Medania
varieties.why: "Excellent" for autumn; came through the hard winter of 2022–23 at Dowding's.

varieties.name: Giant Winter
varieties.why: Gave Dowding better midwinter picking than Medania.

varieties.name: Mikado F1
varieties.why: The only fully hardy (H5) AGM spinach; UK stock not confirmed.

crops.name: Chicory and radicchio
crops.about: Bitter-sweet red and green heads that stand all winter. They're sown in July, so this year buy plants.
crops.grow: Plant into the bed in late summer; cut heads in winter, and the stumps often resprout.
crops.tip: Sow in early July: earlier sowings bolt, later ones don't heart up.

varieties.name: Palla Rossa
varieties.why: Hardy round radicchio; the 506TT selection "stands well" (Dowding).

varieties.name: Pan di Zucchero
varieties.why: Sugarloaf chicory with tall, milder hearts.

varieties.name: Grumolo Verde / Rosso
varieties.why: Very cold-resistant rosettes for picking in late winter.

crops.name: Strawberries
crops.about: Planted now, they root over winter and give a proper crop next June.
crops.grow: Cut an X in the cardboard and plant with the crown sitting exactly at soil level. Too deep and it rots; too high and it dries out.
crops.tip: Net them when the fruit starts to colour, or the birds get there first. Replace the plants every 3–4 years.

varieties.name: Christine
varieties.why: The only early variety resistant to verticillium wilt, which matters on clay. Excellent flavour.

varieties.name: Honeoye
varieties.why: Plentiful harvests of large, firm berries.

varieties.name: Cambridge Favourite
varieties.why: "Very popular and reliable. Good disease resistance" (RHS).

varieties.name: Florence
varieties.why: Late, firm, the best all-round disease profile. Tolerates verticillium.

varieties.name: Symphony
varieties.why: Late with excellent flavour; tolerates red core.

varieties.name: Mara des Bois
varieties.why: Wild-strawberry flavour at full size, mid-August to October.

crops.name: Poached egg plant
crops.about: Low yellow-and-white flowers in late spring. Hoverflies and bees love it, and it seeds itself year after year.
crops.grow: Scatter the seed between the strawberries and press it into the compost. Sow now for flowers in May.
crops.tip: The hoverfly larvae it feeds go on to eat aphids. Let a few plants set seed in summer.

varieties.name: Limnanthes douglasii (the species)
varieties.why: Holds the AGM and has no named selections worth buying. It draws bees and hoverflies and self-seeds.

crops.name: Calendula
crops.about: Pot marigold. Hoverflies come for the flowers and their larvae eat blackfly. The petals are edible.
crops.grow: Sow 1 cm deep in pots in March–April, or straight into the pots outside in April.
crops.tip: Pick off the dead flowers and it flowers until the first frost.

varieties.name: Indian Prince
varieties.why: Large single flowers with open centres: what hoverflies need. On the RHS Plants for Pollinators list.

varieties.name: Calendula officinalis (plain)
varieties.why: The species: single, self-seeding, on the Plants for Pollinators list.

varieties.name: Daisy Mixed
varieties.why: Single, daisy-like flowers in mixed colours.

varieties.name: Fiesta Gitana
varieties.why: The only calendula AGM. Dwarf, good in pots, but its double flowers help hoverflies less.

crops.name: Tomatoes
crops.about: Cherry and bush types suit pots outdoors. Plant them on the sunny south edge after the last frost, which is late May in London.
crops.grow: Sow indoors on a warm windowsill. Pot on once, then into a big pot of compost outside.
crops.tip: Water steadily, since uneven watering splits the fruit. Feed every week once the first flowers open.

varieties.name: Crimson Crush F1
varieties.why: UK-bred cordon with real blight resistance; crops before blight takes it in September.

varieties.name: Mountain Magic F1
varieties.why: Cocktail cordon with the best independent blight evidence (Cornell trials).

varieties.name: Losetto F1
varieties.why: 30 cm bush cherry, very sweet, little pruning; growers report near blight resistance.

varieties.name: Lizzano F1
varieties.why: Semi-trailing 50 cm bush cherry for pots and baskets.

varieties.name: Sungold F1
varieties.why: Fine, refreshing sweetness and ripens early. No blight resistance.

crops.name: Lemon and lime
crops.about: Citrus in pots. They spend the summer on the plot and the winter at home, because a London frost kills them.
crops.grow: Bring them home in October before the first frost and keep them in a bright, cool room. Take them back to the plot in June, once nights stay above 10 °C.
crops.spacing: One tree per 30–40 cm pot, in citrus or loam-based compost
crops.tip: Water when the top few centimetres are dry, less in winter. Feed with citrus food: the summer kind April–September, the winter kind October–March.

varieties.name: Lemon 'Four Seasons'
varieties.why: Flowers and fruits most of the year, self-fertile; nurseries find it better behaved than Meyer.

varieties.name: Meyer lemon
varieties.why: Compact, sweeter fruit, ideal for pots. Dislikes damp autumns, so bring it in early.

varieties.name: Tahiti / Bearss lime
varieties.why: The most reliable fruiting lime for Britain; seedless.

varieties.name: Kaffir (makrut) lime
varieties.why: Grown for its aromatic leaves, so it doesn't matter if it doesn't fruit.

crops.name: Early potatoes
crops.about: First earlies such as Charlotte or Rocket, ready about 12 weeks after planting. They follow the winter salads.
crops.grow: No-dig: set the seed potatoes on the compost and cover them with 10 cm more compost. Add more compost over the shoots as they grow.
crops.tip: Lift them when the flowers open. Earlies are usually out before blight arrives.

varieties.name: Casablanca
varieties.why: Dowding grows it: high yields of clean, smooth tubers, pulled not dug in late June.

varieties.name: Orla
varieties.why: Excellent resistance to blight on leaves and tubers, plus scab.

varieties.name: Sharpe's Express
varieties.why: Classic flavour, said to suit heavy soils.

varieties.name: Maris Bard
varieties.why: Heavy early crops with an earthy flavour.

varieties.name: Red Duke of York
varieties.why: Red skin and great flavour.

varieties.name: Rocket
varieties.why: One of the very earliest, but weak on scab and blight.

crops.name: Courgettes
crops.about: One or two plants is plenty for one person. They follow the broad beans in June.
crops.grow: Sow indoors in April, or outside in late May. Plant into a pocket of compost and water well.
crops.tip: Pick them at 15 cm, every two or three days at the peak, or they turn into marrows.

varieties.name: Tuscany F1
varieties.why: High yields of slender dark fruit; strong powdery mildew resistance (RHS).

varieties.name: Defender F1
varieties.why: Proven heavy cropper, resists cucumber mosaic virus.

varieties.name: Early Gem F1
varieties.why: Dowding: has "grown well for me since 1984".

varieties.name: Sure Thing F1
varieties.why: Compact and bred for mildew resistance.

crops.name: Winter squash
crops.about: Trailing plants with fruit that keeps for months. An alternative to courgettes after the beans.
crops.grow: Sow indoors in late April. Plant out in early June into a pocket of compost and let it trail along the path edge.
crops.tip: Leave the fruit on the plant until the skin is hard, then cure it in the sun for a week before storing.

varieties.name: Uchiki Kuri
varieties.why: Ripens even in damp summers, excellent flavour, keeps until about January.

varieties.name: Crown Prince F1
varieties.why: Superb flavour and the best keeper, often until April. Ripens a little later.

varieties.name: Honey Bear F1
varieties.why: Compact bush acorn squash for a small plot.

varieties.name: Hunter / Harrier
varieties.why: The only AGM butternuts, but butternuts need a hot summer to ripen.

crops.name: Leeks
crops.about: Planted in midsummer, they stand in the ground all winter until you need them.
crops.grow: Sow in modules in March. In June make a 15 cm hole with a dibber through the compost, drop a leek in, fill the hole with water and don't backfill.
crops.tip: Leek moth and rust are about in London. Insect mesh in summer helps with the moth.

varieties.name: Oarsman F1
varieties.why: British-bred, straight and uniform, stands well; tolerates rust.

varieties.name: Bandit
varieties.why: Late leek to pick from winter into spring; said to resist rust.

varieties.name: Porbella
varieties.why: Long cropping season with thick white stems.

varieties.name: Toledo
varieties.why: Long shanks for use November to March.

varieties.name: Musselburgh
varieties.why: Very hardy Scottish heritage leek; you can save the seed.

crops.name: Kale
crops.about: Cavolo nero or curly kale. You pick it leaf by leaf all winter.
crops.grow: Sow in modules in April–May. Plant firmly into the compost in June–July.
crops.tip: Net it against pigeons and cabbage white butterflies from the day you plant it.

varieties.name: Reflex F1
varieties.why: Blue-green curly kale that keeps its colour in cold; long harvest.

varieties.name: Redbor F1
varieties.why: Very curly red-purple leaves over a long period.

varieties.name: Starbor F1
varieties.why: Compact and needs no staking: good for a late planting.

varieties.name: Nero di Toscana
varieties.why: "Probably the tastiest" (Dowding), but less frost-hardy and attracts whitefly.

varieties.name: Red Russian
varieties.why: Tender leaves good raw; growers find it gets less whitefly.

crops.name: Borlotti beans
crops.about: A climbing bean with red-speckled pods. Eat them fresh in late summer or dry them for winter.
crops.grow: Sow indoors in late April, or outside in late May at the foot of a wigwam on the north side, where it won't shade the bed.
crops.spacing: Two plants per cane, canes 30 cm apart
crops.tip: For dried beans, leave the pods on the plant until they rattle.

varieties.name: Lingua di Fuoco (climbing)
varieties.why: RHS-recommended for drying. Pods ripen mottled pink, about 1.8 m. Check the packet says climbing, not 'Nano'.

varieties.name: Borlotto Lamon
varieties.why: The bean for pasta e fagioli; 1.8–2 m.

varieties.name: Borlotto Stregonta
varieties.why: Italian climber with long streaked seeds, about 80 days.

crops.name: French beans
crops.about: Dwarf French beans fit where the garlic and onions come out in July.
crops.grow: Sow 5 cm deep straight into the compost once the soil is warm. A July sowing crops until the first frost.
crops.tip: Pick them small and often; the more you pick, the more they make.

varieties.name: Stanley
varieties.why: High yields; said to resist halo blight, anthracnose and bean mosaic virus.

varieties.name: Sprite
varieties.why: Totally stringless straight dark pods, compact, needs no support.

varieties.name: Elba
varieties.why: Long green pods (Dowding).

varieties.name: Tendergreen
varieties.why: Stringless and early: good for a late July sowing.

catalog.varietiesNote: Varieties researched in October 2026. AGM is the RHS Award of Garden Merit; claims made only by a seed seller are marked. On clay, how you grow (mesh, mulch, November sowing, module plugs) matters more than which variety.
